concepts.label: SQL++
concepts.reused_or_minted: reused - already promoted (alias n1ql:sql-plus-plus); this page is the comparison-against-SQL angle of the same language.

concepts.label: SQL (relational query language)
concepts.reused_or_minted: minted - no existing concept for standard relational SQL anywhere in the registry; this page treats it as SQL++'s comparison partner throughout.

concepts.label: keyspace
concepts.reused_or_minted: minted - 'keyspace' is used constantly elsewhere in the registry's n1ql:* definitions (e.g. n1ql:query-context, n1ql:select) but was never itself promoted as a concept; this page defines it directly against the relational table.

concepts.label: table (relational)
concepts.reused_or_minted: minted - the relational counterpart to n1ql:keyspace, named explicitly on this page as having 'uniform structure'.

concepts.label: collection/construction operator (SQL++ projection)
concepts.reused_or_minted: minted - the page's own term for projection-time object/array reshaping expressions (e.g. `{'FullTime': true} AS 'Status'`); no existing n1ql:* statement or clause concept covers this.

concepts.label: IS MISSING operator
concepts.reused_or_minted: minted - distinct from n1ql:scan-consistency's enum and from any existing statement; this is the operator distinguishing an absent field from an explicit null.

concepts.label: ANY / SOME / EVERY operators
concepts.reused_or_minted: minted - array-predicate operator family named explicitly on the page, not covered by n1ql:aggregate-functions or n1ql:misc-utility-functions.

concepts.label: dot / square-bracket nested-element accessor
concepts.reused_or_minted: minted - the dot and square-bracket syntax for descending into a document's nested elements/arrays, distinct from FROM/keyspace-level access.

relations.subject: n1ql:sqlpp
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: minted - no existing predicate expresses a top-level language-vs-language structural comparison; tradesOffAgainst is for two strategies with opposing strengths, not this kind of foundational data-model contrast.
relations.evidence: The most important difference between SQL++ and SQL is the _data model_.

relations.subject: n1ql:keyspace
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - same minted predicate as above, applied one level down to the concrete data-container pair.
relations.evidence: By contrast, SQL++ handles data as free-form documents, gathered into large collections called _keyspaces_. There is no uniformity; nor is there any logical proximity shared by objects of the same _data shape_ within the keyspace.

relations.subject: n1ql:sqlpp
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - existing predicate, exact shape fit ('the subject supports the named language construct or dialect feature').
relations.evidence: an arbitrary expression in the projection may contain collection operators or construction operators, which enable you to reshape the data in ways that go beyond merely adding an extra field

relations.subject: n1ql:sqlpp
relations.evidence: SQL++ provides a complementary set of operators like `IS MISSING`, in addition to standard operators like `IS NULL`.

relations.subject: n1ql:sqlpp
relations.evidence: SQL++ provides new operators to work with arrays in documents: `ANY`, `SOME`, and `EVERY`.

relations.subject: n1ql:sqlpp
relations.evidence: Such nested elements are addressed using the dot (.) operator to descend a level, and the square-bracket ( \[ \] ) operator to index into an array element.

cross_component_finding: This page never names hasNoRelationshipTo/shouldNotBeConfusedWith/doesNotSupport explicitly, despite the round brief flagging it as a likely source for those - the text contains no 'does not' or 'cannot' sentence anywhere. Every contrast here is phrased positively ('SQL++ provides X, in addition to Y'), so I did not force a negative-relation predicate onto it; the comparison is real but the page's own phrasing is additive, not exclusionary. This is itself worth recording: not every comparison page yields negative relations, only ones that state a boundary in the negative.
